command_words.definition: Carefully consider the construction and crafting of your text within the context of a first draft.
Carefully consider your effective use of language, structural, stylistic and generic features within the context of a first draft. Functionally close to "compose," but slightly foregrounds technique.
To produce or invent a text.
Functionally interchangeable with the above in composing questions; no separate formal definition, but still implies deliberate construction, not a rough note.

text_types.definition: Texts whose primary purpose is to entertain or provoke thought through imaginative use of literary elements; recognised for form, style and artistic/aesthetic value (novels, stories, plays, poetry, film).
Texts whose primary purpose is to explain and interpret personalities, events, ideas, representations or concepts (autobiography, biography, feature articles, documentary, satire, allegory).
Texts whose primary purpose is to put forward a viewpoint and persuade a reader, viewer or listener (advertising, debates, arguments, discussions, polemics, essays).

Texts whose primary purpose is to identify, examine and draw conclusions about the elements of other texts (commentaries, essays in criticism, reviews). Rare as a composing-question type, but useful to recognise.

key_concept_terms.definition: A sense of beauty or an appreciation of artistic expression.
An outlook or specific feeling about something; underpinned by values, expressed through what we say, do and wear.
The group of readers, listeners or viewers being addressed; includes an implied audience, not just a literal one.
The composer or originator of a work.
The environment in which a text is created or received; can be the context of culture (broad social/historical/cultural conditions) or the context of situation (the text's immediate environment).
An accepted practice developed over time and generally understood — the techniques, features or elements that belong to a genre.
Word groups used in a non-literal way for effect (simile, metaphor, personification).
The shape and structure of a text (novel, poem, monologue, feature article, etc.).
The category a text belongs to, distinguished by subject matter, form or structure.
Composite texts mixing elements from different sources or genres (e.g. infotainment, or email mixing talk and print conventions).
Understandings, thoughts, notions, opinions, views or beliefs — open in meaning within this course.
The meaning made of a text; different reading strategies can produce different interpretations.
Matters of personal or public concern that are in dispute or directly/indirectly affect people.
Literal: the physical features of an area of land (terrain, vegetation, natural elements). Figurative: the broader setting or context of a situation (can also mean urban/city/seascapes).
Features supporting meaning: sentence structure, vocabulary, punctuation, figurative language, and similar.
The arrangement of repeated, alternating or contrasting elements in a text (a recurring chorus, a call-and-response structure, opposing imagery).
Language used to discuss language (e.g. "characterisation," "mise-en-scène," "clause").
The processes of communication (listening, speaking, reading/viewing, writing/creating), or the semiotic resources tied to them (sound, print, image, gesture).
The atmosphere or feeling of a text (sombre, exhilarating, menacing).
A text combining two or more communication modes (e.g. print + image + spoken text in film).
A story of real or imagined events or experiences.
How a narrator relates to the story (first/third person, omniscient/restricted, reliable/unreliable).
A position from which things are viewed; more than an opinion — a viewpoint informed by context.
Describing an inanimate object as though it were alive.
Ordinary written/spoken language, without poetry's marked metrical structure.
The way people, events, issues or subjects are presented in a text — texts construct "reality," they don't mirror it.
The language of argument, using persuasive and forceful language.
Techniques used in argument to persuade (rhetorical questions, repetition, figurative language).
The variety of English used in more formal Australian settings; dynamic but recognised as the "common language."
The culmination of distinctive qualities that characterise a text (or a body of work, or a period).
The selection of stylistic features to achieve a particular effect.
The features contributing to a text's style: lexical choice, syntax, point of view, voice, structure, composition, language patterns.
A literary device where a tangible object, character or event represents something more abstract (a concept, theme, emotion).
How information is organised in a text type (headings, sequencing, topic sentences, sonnets, monologues).
An idea, concern or argument developed in a text; a work may have more than one.
The way "voice" is delivered — friendly, angry, persuasive, and so on.
Composition, framing, shot size, camera angle, and other visual components of a text.
The distinct personality discernible in a text, constructed through language and stylistic choices; a text can contain multiple voices.

hinge_words.definition: "Essential, necessary, or a vital part of a whole." Test: if you removed this element, would the theme/character arc still work? If yes, it wasn't integral.
Clearly recognisable, setting something apart from others of its kind. Test: could this description apply to almost any text of this genre, or only to yours specifically?
Unusual or unexpected for its type; not what would normally be expected in that genre or context. Test: would a reader be surprised, given the genre's normal conventions?
Not anticipated by the audience, given the setup. Test: does the text actively set up an expectation first, so the swerve actually registers as unexpected?
A concrete object/event standing in for something abstract. Test: does the symbol recur or develop, or does it appear once and do nothing more?

"To be influenced, motivated or guided by." You are not required to directly reference the stimulus — just show a clear, identifiable link. Test: could a reader trace your text back to the stimulus, even loosely?

To contain or use as part of a whole; "captured" specifically means depicted or illustrated in a given image or scenario. Test: is the situation actually present and doing work in your text, or just mentioned in passing?
Retaining, protecting for future generations, restoring, or otherwise maintaining for posterity. Test: does your text argue for keeping/restoring something, not just describe it fondly?
